abstract: Prescription opioids like oxycodone (OXY; the active component in OxyContin) continue to drive the ongoing opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic due to their widespread prescription and distribution. Genetic factors influencing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of opioids can have profound impacts on drug response and, in turn, influence risk for OUD. We previously used quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and gene validation to identify zinc-finger homeobox 2 (Zhx2) loss-of-function as a quantitative trait gene and mechanism underlying increased brain concentration of oxymorphone (OMOR) following systemic administration of OXY in BALB/cJ females that was linked to increased OXY reward. To test whether we could rescue the behavioral phenotype, we overexpressed Zhx2 in the brain via retro-orbital injection of a brain-specific adeno-associated virus (AAV). We observed restricted Zhx2 expression (especially females), with more widespread expression in males. Consequently, we did not observe any significant effect of brain Zhx2 overexpression on OXY reward as measured via conditioned place preference (CPP). However, Zhx2 overexpression did protect against OXY-induced weight loss in females following a high-dose OXY regimen. Despite the effect on weight loss, Zhx2 overexpression had no effect on spontaneous or naloxone-precipitated withdrawal behaviors. We then examined native Zhx2 protein expression in the brains of the BALB/cByJ substrain (showing wild-type levels of Zhx2 expression) via immunohistochemical co-localization and found that Zhx2 is mainly expressed in neurons located in key reward, motivational, and emotion-related regions such as the hippocampus (HPC), amygdala, striatum (Str), and cerebellum. To summarize, Zhx2 overexpression via retro-orbital AAV administration was quite limited, yet had significant effects on opioid-induced weight loss. Furthermore, for the first time, we provide anatomical visualization of Zhx2 expression at the protein level in neurons vs. glia throughout multiple brain regions.
